paragraphs.text: This is the Ravi river in northern India, in the autumn of 2018. Now watch the same bend in October 2026.
A new dam, Shahpurkandi, finished in 2024.
India built it to keep water that used to flow on, downstream, into Pakistan.
Under a treaty from 1960, that is India's right. The Ravi is one of three rivers the treaty gave to India.
Three bigger rivers went to Pakistan. And in April 2025, India said it would hold that whole treaty in abeyance.

stat.label: India puts the Indus Waters Treaty "in abeyance"

paragraphs.text: Pakistan answered the next day. Any attempt to stop or divert its water, it said, would be an act of war.

shots.photo: File:India-Pakistan Border at Night.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The India-Pakistan border at night, from the Space Station

shots.quote: Any attempt to stop or divert the flow of water belonging to Pakistan … will be considered as an Act of War.
shots.author: National Security Committee of Pakistan, April 24, 2025

paragraphs.text: In August 2026, a court in The Hague ruled that the treaty is still fully in force.

shots.photo: File:Den Haag, het Vredespaleis RM333074 IMG 4317 2024-08-05 10.02.jpg

paragraphs.text: India rejected the ruling within hours, and called the court illegal.

stat.label: India's answer to the court's award
stat.note: India has not taken part in the case

paragraphs.text: So can one country really turn off another country's rivers?

ask.text: Can one country turn off another's rivers?

paragraphs.text: And why did a deal that survived three wars break now? It starts with a single morning in 1948.

shots.photo: File:Marala shutters (1915).jpg

paragraphs.text: When British India was split in 1947, the new border cut straight through the Punjab.
Punjab means the land of five rivers, and the new line cut across them.
Most of the rivers rose in India, or ran through it first.
Many of the farms they watered ended up in Pakistan, fed by canals that began on the Indian side.
For a few months, a standstill agreement kept the canals running.

shots.photo: File:Marala shutters (1915).jpg

paragraphs.text: It had been signed in December 1947. It ran out on March 31st, 1948.

stat.label: the canal standstill agreement runs out

paragraphs.text: The next morning, East Punjab, now in India, shut the water off.
Canals fed from the Indian side, like the Dipalpur canal from Ferozepur, went dry in Pakistan.
Lahore, a city that drew its water from those canals, felt it at once.
About five and a half percent of Pakistan's cropland faced a growing season with no water.

stat.label: of Pakistan's cropland facing a season without water

paragraphs.text: The water came back after about five weeks, once Pakistan agreed to talks.
It agreed to pay for the water, and later said it had signed under duress.

stat.label: how Pakistan later described the May 1948 deal

paragraphs.text: Under that deal, East Punjab would slowly reduce the canal water, so that Pakistan could find other sources.
Pakistan never forgot that its rivers could be shut off from upstream.
Keep that morning in mind, because it is the fear behind everything that follows.

shots.photo: File:India-Pakistan Border at Night.jpg

paragraphs.text: In 1951, David Lilienthal, who had run America's Tennessee Valley Authority, toured both countries.
He proposed that the two countries develop the Indus together, with the World Bank's help.
Sharing one river system turned out to be impossible.

shots.photo: File:Indus River above Hyderabad photographed during MA-9 flight (S63-06455).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The Indus above Hyderabad, from Mercury-Atlas 9, May 1963

paragraphs.text: So in 1954, the World Bank proposed something simpler: split it.

stat.label: the World Bank proposes splitting the rivers

paragraphs.text: The three eastern rivers, the Ravi, the Beas and the Sutlej, would go to India.
The three western ones, the Indus, the Jhelum and the Chenab, would go to Pakistan.
It took six more years of talks. The two leaders met at Windsor Castle in May 1960.

shots.photo: File:Queen Elizabeth II and the Prime Ministers of the Commonwealth Nations, at Windsor Castle (1960 Commonwealth Prime Minister's Conference).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Nehru (front row) and Ayub Khan (back row) at Windsor Castle, May 1960

paragraphs.text: On September 19th, 1960, in Karachi, they signed it: India's prime minister Jawaharlal Nehru and Pakistan's president Ayub Khan.

stat.label: the Indus Waters Treaty is signed in Karachi
stat.note: With W. A. B. Iliff for the World Bank

paragraphs.text: The split was not even. The eastern rivers carry about 33 million acre-feet of water in an average year.

chart.title: Average yearly flow (million acre-feet)
chart.source: Indus Waters Treaty figures, via Wikipedia

paragraphs.text: The western rivers carry about 135 million. So Pakistan got roughly four fifths of the water.
India got the rivers closest to its farms, and full use of them.
On the western rivers, India kept some rights. It may build hydropower plants in Kashmir,
as long as they let the river flow through, and it may store only a limited amount.
It may also irrigate up to about 701,000 acres of farmland from them.

stat.label: acres India may irrigate from the western rivers

paragraphs.text: That limit is about 3.6 million acre-feet in total, for storage, power and floods. Remember that number.

stat.label: acre-feet: the most India may store on the western rivers

paragraphs.text: Pakistan now had to build canals to replace the eastern rivers it lost.
India agreed to pay about 62 million pounds toward that, over ten years.

stat.label: paid by India toward Pakistan's new works

paragraphs.text: And for a ten-year transition, while the new canals were dug, India kept sending eastern water across.
The rest came from abroad. On the same day, six countries and the World Bank signed a fund to pay for it.

stat.label: pledged by the United States in 1960
stat.note: With Australia, Canada, West Germany, New Zealand, the UK and the World Bank

paragraphs.text: The money built two of the biggest dams of the age. Mangla, on the Jhelum, opened in 1967.

shots.photo: File:Mangla-Panorama.jpg

paragraphs.text: And Tarbela, on the Indus itself, was finished in 1976.
It is one of the largest earth-filled dams in the world.

shots.photo: File:Tarbela Dam spillway DSC 4280 (5835435528).jpg

paragraphs.text: Link canals now carry western water east, to the farms that had lost the eastern rivers.
Most of Pakistan's farm output depends on this one irrigation system.

shots.photo: File:Indus River above Hyderabad photographed during MA-9 flight (S63-06455).jpg

paragraphs.text: Pakistan's government calls the rivers a lifeline for 240 million people.

stat.label: people Pakistan says depend on these rivers
stat.source: National Security Committee of Pakistan, April 2025

paragraphs.text: We map rivers like this from orbit in every episode. If you want to see which river we follow next, subscribe.
The treaty set up a Permanent Indus Commission, one commissioner from each side.
They meet at least once a year, swap river data and inspect each other's works.

shots.photo: File:Rockfill Dam, Salal Hydroelectric Power Station, Jammu.jpg

paragraphs.text: India and Pakistan went to war in 1965, again in 1971, and fought in Kargil in 1999.

stat.label: the Indus Commission kept working through

paragraphs.text: The water kept flowing, and the commission kept meeting, 118 times in all.
The fights moved to the drawing board instead: how India designs its dams on Pakistan's rivers.
Salal, on the Chenab, was settled by agreement in 1978.
The bigger Baglihar dam, upstream, went to a neutral expert, who cleared it.

shots.photo: File:Baglihar Dam Chenab River J&K India.jpg

paragraphs.text: Then came Kishanganga. This is the Gurez valley in Kashmir in 2014. Now watch the same valley in 2026.

shots.photo: File:Tranquil Beauty of Gurez Valley.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The Kishanganga river in the Gurez valley

paragraphs.text: A dam, and a lake behind it.
The dam sends the river into a 23-kilometre tunnel, through the mountains,
to a power plant that drains into Wular Lake, on the Jhelum.
Downstream, the same river crosses into Pakistan as the Neelum.
Pakistan had built a 969 megawatt plant of its own there, and needed that water.

stat.label: Pakistan's Neelum-Jhelum plant, downstream

paragraphs.text: Experts estimated that Kishanganga would cost that plant about a tenth of its water.
India's prime minister Narendra Modi opened Kishanganga in May 2018.
By then a court of arbitration had ruled. India could divert water for power,

shots.photo: File:Den Haag, het Vredespaleis RM333074 IMG 4317 2024-08-05 10.02.jpg

paragraphs.text: but must always leave at least nine cubic metres a second in the river.

stat.label: the least Kishanganga must always leave in the river

paragraphs.text: Look at the river below the dam: a thin thread.
That was the system working as designed. Each side won a little, and the treaty held.
By 2016, the disputes were piling up again, over Kishanganga and over a new dam on the Chenab, at Ratle.
Ratle is an 850 megawatt plant behind a 133-metre dam.
Pakistan objects to its design: how much water it can hold back, and where its gates sit.

stat.label: Ratle hydroelectric plant on the Chenab

paragraphs.text: That September, militants attacked an Indian army base at Uri, in Kashmir.
Narendra Modi told officials that blood and water cannot flow together.

shots.quote: Blood and water cannot flow together.
shots.author: Narendra Modi, September 2016, as reported

paragraphs.text: India suspended the commission's meetings for a time.

stat.label: Indus Commission meetings, after the Uri attack

paragraphs.text: Pakistan asked for a court of arbitration. India asked for a neutral expert instead.

shots.photo: File:Den Haag, het Vredespaleis RM333074 IMG 4317 2024-08-05 10.02.jpg

paragraphs.text: The World Bank could not choose between them, so it paused both, for six years.

stat.label: the World Bank pauses both processes

paragraphs.text: When the process restarted in 2022, it ran on two tracks at once.
India boycotted the court. It argued that running a court alongside the expert broke the treaty's step-by-step dispute process.

stat.label: India asks Pakistan to modify the treaty

paragraphs.text: In 2024, it went further, and asked for a full review, citing population growth, clean energy needs and terrorism.

stat.label: India asks for a review of the whole treaty

paragraphs.text: The commission met for the last time in May 2022. Even before 2025, the treaty was barely breathing.

stat.label: the last meeting of the Permanent Indus Commission

paragraphs.text: Then came a single attack. And what came next is the part most people outside the region missed.
On April 22nd, 2025, gunmen killed 26 people near Pahalgam, in Indian-administered Kashmir. Most were tourists.

stat.label: people killed near Pahalgam

paragraphs.text: The next day, India held the treaty in abeyance, with immediate effect.

shots.quote: The Indus Waters Treaty of 1960 will be held in abeyance with immediate effect …
shots.author: Government of India, April 23, 2025

paragraphs.text: It would last, India said, until Pakistan credibly and irrevocably abjures support for cross-border terrorism. Pakistan denied any role in the attack.

shots.photo: File:India-Pakistan Border at Night.jpg

stat.label: Pakistan rejects any role in the attack

paragraphs.text: Within days, India flushed silt from its Salal reservoir,
and from Baglihar, out of season and without telling Pakistan.
To flush a reservoir you first empty it, and then you refill it.

shots.photo: File:Baglihar Dam Chenab River J&K India.jpg

paragraphs.text: Downstream, at Pakistan's Marala headworks, the Chenab enters the country.
Pakistani officials said the river fell from about 35,600 cubic feet a second to about 3,200, overnight.

chart.title: Chenab at Marala (cubic feet a second)

paragraphs.text: Other readings that week were higher, and the flow came back.
But Pakistan had seen what a switch upstream could do.
Reuters reported that India had started work to get more out of its Chenab plants.
On May 7th the two countries went to war for four days, with missiles and drones,
until a ceasefire on May 10th. The treaty stayed in abeyance.

stat.label: of fighting between India and Pakistan

paragraphs.text: Bilawal Bhutto Zardari, a former foreign minister, warned that Pakistan would secure its water from all six rivers.

shots.quote: Either India shares water fairly or we will secure it from all six rivers.
shots.author: Bilawal Bhutto Zardari, June 2025, as reported by Dawn

paragraphs.text: That August, Pakistan's army chief, Asim Munir, was reported to say that Pakistan would destroy any Indian dam built to block the Indus.

shots.photo: File:Tarbela Dam spillway DSC 4280 (5835435528).jpg

stat.label: Asim Munir's reported threat against any such dam

paragraphs.text: India stopped sharing river data.
Yet that August, when the Tawi river was about to flood, it warned Pakistan anyway,
through its High Commission, on humanitarian grounds.

stat.label: India warns Pakistan of a Tawi flood, outside the treaty

paragraphs.text: Pakistan said even that broke the treaty, because the warning should have come through the Indus commission.
Pakistan took the fight to the court of arbitration that India was boycotting.

shots.photo: File:Den Haag, het Vredespaleis RM333074 IMG 4317 2024-08-05 10.02.jpg

paragraphs.text: In June 2025, the court said India's abeyance could not take away its power to hear the case.

stat.label: the court keeps the case despite the abeyance

paragraphs.text: That August, it set the general rule. India shall let the western rivers flow, for Pakistan's unrestricted use.

shots.quote: India shall "let flow" the waters of the Western Rivers for Pakistan's unrestricted use.
shots.author: Court of Arbitration, August 8, 2025, as summarised

paragraphs.text: Exceptions, like hydropower, must be read strictly.
In May 2026, it ruled on how much water India's plants may hold back each day.

stat.label: the court's award on maximum pondage

paragraphs.text: Then Pakistan asked the big question: is the treaty still alive at all?

shots.photo: File:Den Haag, het Vredespaleis RM333074 IMG 4317 2024-08-05 10.02.jpg

paragraphs.text: Hearings ran for three days in April 2026. India did not take part.

stat.label: hearings at the Peace Palace, without India

paragraphs.text: Pakistan's case was led by Sir Daniel Bethlehem, a British lawyer. The court is chaired by an American professor, Sean Murphy.

shots.photo: File:Den Haag, het Vredespaleis RM333074 IMG 4317 2024-08-05 10.02.jpg

stat.label: chaired by Prof. Sean D. Murphy
stat.note: Belgium, the US, Jordan and Australia

paragraphs.text: On August 31st, 2026, five judges answered, unanimously.

stat.label: "The Indus Waters Treaty remains fully in force"
stat.source: Court of Arbitration, PCA press release

paragraphs.text: None of India's reasons could suspend or end the treaty. It remains fully in force.
The same day, the court ordered India not to raise the Ratle dam wall above certain levels,
until 90 days after the neutral expert decides, which is expected in July 2027.

stat.label: the neutral expert's decision on Ratle and Kishanganga

paragraphs.text: India rejected it within hours. It calls the court illegally constituted.

stat.label: India calls the court "illegally constituted"
stat.source: Ministry of External Affairs; Al Jazeera

paragraphs.text: For India, the treaty stays in abeyance.
And there is no police force for this ruling. No one can make India comply.

shots.photo: File:Den Haag, het Vredespaleis RM333074 IMG 4317 2024-08-05 10.02.jpg

paragraphs.text: So who is right, a court that India never agreed to appear before,

shots.photo: File:India-Pakistan Border at Night.jpg

paragraphs.text: or a government that says the other side broke the deal first?

ask.text: The court, or India's government: who is right?

chapters.title: Can India Turn Off the Indus?

paragraphs.text: Here is the physical answer, for now. The western rivers are huge in summer, when Himalayan snow melts.
And India's dams on them were built to let water through, not to hold it.
Pakistani hydrologist Hassan Abbas puts India's built storage on the Chenab at roughly one million acre-feet.

stat.label: acre-feet of storage India has built on the Chenab

paragraphs.text: That is small against what Pakistan's farms take in a season.
If India held the river back behind dams that small, he says, it would end up flooding itself.
For now, he argues, Pakistan's rivers are protected less by the treaty than by geography.

shots.photo: File:Tranquil Beauty of Gurez Valley.jpg

paragraphs.text: But timing is another matter. In the dry months the rivers run low.
Even a few days of holding back, or a sudden release, can hit Pakistani farms at sowing time.

shots.photo: File:Indus River above Hyderabad photographed during MA-9 flight (S63-06455).jpg

paragraphs.text: And India is building. Pakistani reporting says the hydropower planned in India's Chenab basin
rose from about 3,300 megawatts to about 7,600 in eighteen months.

chart.title: Hydropower planned in India's Chenab basin

paragraphs.text: That includes Sawalkot, an 1,856 megawatt plant.

stat.label: Sawalkot, planned on the Chenab

paragraphs.text: The same reports say India tendered a tunnel in March 2026, to link the Chenab to the Beas, an eastern river.
Pakistani analysts say that link could move up to 1.9 million acre-feet a year.

stat.label: acre-feet a year the Chenab-Beas link could divert
stat.note: Pakistani estimate; not confirmed by India

paragraphs.text: India has not published those figures, and none of it can be built quickly in these mountains.

shots.photo: File:Tranquil Beauty of Gurez Valley.jpg

paragraphs.text: India has also sent plans to rebuild the Ranbir canal, which draws on the Chenab near Jammu.
The treaty's limit was 3.6 million acre-feet of storage. Out of the treaty, India would have no limit at all.

stat.label: acre-feet: the treaty's storage limit for India

paragraphs.text: That is why Pakistan fears tomorrow more than today.
Pakistan's prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, has called every drop of its water a red line.

shots.quote: Every single drop of Pakistan's water is our red line.
shots.author: Shehbaz Sharif, August 13, 2026

paragraphs.text: India's foreign minister says the treaty stays suspended until Pakistan stops cross-border terrorism.
In June 2026, Pakistan's defence minister, Khawaja Asif, threatened war over it. India's foreign ministry dismissed the remarks.

stat.label: Pakistan's defence minister threatens war over the water

paragraphs.text: India argues a treaty from 1960 never planned for today's populations, or for clean energy.

shots.photo: File:Rockfill Dam, Salal Hydroelectric Power Station, Jammu.jpg

paragraphs.text: Pakistan says India must first return to the treaty, which can only be changed if both sides agree.
In the meantime, the rivers keep running, past dams on one side and canals on the other,

shots.photo: File:Indus River above Hyderabad photographed during MA-9 flight (S63-06455).jpg

paragraphs.text: on to the Arabian Sea.
The next real date is July 2027, when the neutral expert rules on Ratle and Kishanganga.

stat.label: the neutral expert's final decision

paragraphs.text: India asked for that expert in 2016. Whether it accepts his ruling now is the next test.
So here is our question for you. Should a water treaty be untouchable, even in war,

shots.photo: File:India-Pakistan Border at Night.jpg

ask.text: Untouchable treaty, or the right to walk away?

paragraphs.text: or can a country walk away when it believes its neighbour is attacking it?

youtube.title: India Froze a 65-Year-Old Water Treaty With Pakistan
youtube.description:
In April 2025 India put the Indus Waters Treaty "in abeyance". Pakistan said stopping its water would be an act of war. In August 2026 a court in The Hague ruled the treaty is still fully in force, and India rejected the ruling within hours. We follow the six rivers from the day the canals ran dry in 1948 to the new dams on the Chenab, with real satellite images, and ask whether India could actually turn off Pakistan's water.

Real Copernicus Sentinel-2 images, NASA photographs, Natural Earth river maps and the court's own documents.
youtube.pinned_comment: Should a water treaty be untouchable, even in war, or can a country walk away when it believes its neighbour is attacking it?
